newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat reiterates sales set for rise in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Fiat reiterates sales set for rise in 1997.

text.p: Fiat on Monday said that its 1997 sales would rise around 15 percent from the previous year while its pretax profits would at least match that of 1996.

Cesare Romiti, chairman of Italy's largest private industrial group, told shareholders at Fiat's annual meeting that 1997 revenues should reach around 90 trillion lire, and despite the absence of extraordinary gains, income before taxes should not be less than in 1996.

"The results achieved thus far....point to an overall improvement in the group's operating and financial performance compared with 1996," he told shareholders at an annual assembly at Fiat's home town here in northwestern Italy.

He added that 1997 operating income before financial and extraordinary items and taxes should be considerably higher than in 1996 both in percentage and absolute terms. The group's financial position should be positive, indicating that the group would move into a net cash position, he said.
Last month, Romiti had indicated that group sales in 1997 would rise around 15 percent and profits for the year would not be below those seen in 1996.
In 1996, Fiat's sales rose four percent to 78 trillion lire, to give operating income from industrial activities of 2.1 trillion lire and income before taxes of 3.8 trillion lire.

The 1996 figures were given a big boost by around 1.4 trillion lire of extraordinary gains from the flotation of 31 percent of New Holland and the sale of fund management group Prime to insurer Generali.

However, Romiti warned that 1997 would be an exacting year with strong uncertainties, with economic recovery in most European countries barely able to get off the ground due to persisting weakness in consumer demand and high unemployment.

He added there was still a lack of confidence owing to uncertainties about the future of Europe's economic and monetary union and the sporadic trend in manufacturing activity, with the economic situation in Italy particularly fragile.

Looking at the group's different sectors, Romiti said the western European car market slipped 4.2 percent on a unit sales basis in the first five months of 1997, and would have been worse except for a 27.9 percent gain in Italy, boosted by a national car buying incentive purchase scheme.

Fiat Auto sales rose 8.2 percent to 1.12 million cars worldwide in the first five months, with the only area of weakness being western Europe, excluding Italy, where Fiat sales were off 18.1 percent due to weak consumer demand.

Romiti said the results in the first five months pushed Fiat's market share in Europe to 12.6 percent to move Fiat from fifth position in the European car industry league in 1996 to second in 1997 behind leader Volkswagen.

In commercial vehicles, Fiat's Iveco heavy trucks units saw sales dip 8.8 percent in the first four months of 1997 to 37,900 units and its share of the European truck market decline to 18.4 percent from 20 percent previously.
Romiti blamed the decline on recession in the truck market due to stagnation of the European economy and delays in the start up of major infrastructure projects.

Fiat's 69-percent owned New Holland agricutural and industrial machinery maker saw tractor sales in the first four months of 1997 up 16.1 percent at 7,200 units, with the European tractor market increasing slightly while the market remained buoyant in North America.
